item.title: Combining a Modified Emergency Severity Index Score with Chief Complaints - Validation of a New Allocation Algorithm for Integrated Emergency Centers
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Objectives: Current health policy reforms in Europe aim to synchronize emergency departments and acute outpatient clinics (AOC)/primary care services through the establishment of Integrated Emergency Centers (IECs). A central challenge of this model is the upstream triage at a central point of assessment (CPA). To date, there is a lack of standardized concepts for a single-stage assessment conducted by emergency-qualified staff that also facilitates cross-sectoral allocation. To address this gap, this study introduces the optimized leading-symptom-weighted modified Emergency Severity Index (L-mESI opt.) triage instrument. This tool aims to safely distribute the clinical workload between emergency departments (EDs) and AOCs by linking a modified emergency severity index (mESI)-omitting vital signs-with the patient's chief complaint (CEDIS).

Methods: A retrospective analysis of walk-in emergency patients was conducted at two university hospitals in 2024 (training dataset: n = 26,845). Outpatient treatment rates were determined for combinations of chief complaints and mESI categories. These probabilities informed an optimized allocation algorithm (L-mESI opt.) via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and the maximum Youden Index. The model was verified using a separate validation dataset (n = 11,512).

Results: The pretest probability for AOC allocation was identified at 74%. The optimized L-mESI-opt. algorithm correctly allocated 54.2% of patients to the AOC, the ED workload was reduced by 46.9%. Compared with standard ESI-based steering, the L-mESI-opt. significantly improved sensitivity for inpatient care from 54.5% to 69.5% and achieved a negative predictive value of 85.4%. Although 14.6% of AOC-allocated patients required subsequent ED admission ("Upstream") in the validation set, critical outcomes remained minimal (observation unit transfer: 0.3%; mortality: 0.1%). Validation confirmed consistent quality and safety.

Conclusion: L-mESI opt. model demonstrates the potential to effectively reduce ED workload while maintaining high patient safety in a simulated environment. These results show that its adaptability could allow for broad application in IECs. However, the successful implementation of such an algorithm will likely depend on close spatial and organizational links between EDs and AOCs to manage bilateral patient flow efficiently. Prospective clinical trials are warranted to confirm these findings in real-world settings.

Schunk D, Balandin A, Kersebaum JN, Aleknonyte-Resch M, Lepsien A, Busch HJ

item.title: An Emergency Department and Emergency Medical Services Superutilizer - A Case Report of a Multidisciplinary Approach to Resolution
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Frequent emergency department (ED) visitors, referred to as high-need, high-cost, or "superutilizers," are a challenging population for the health care system. Superutilizers account for a disproportionate share of overall health care spending (5% of the population accounts for 50% of health care spending) and have therefore been a focus of research and intervention over the past decade. Although ED superutilizers have been described previously, we report a case that demonstrates the additional strain on the emergency medical services (EMS). A 65-year-old woman was the highest 9-1-1 caller for a major metropolitan area, averaging 1.6 transports per day. Identifying the root causes of a patient's frequent utilization can be difficult and sometimes requires stepping back, gaining a fresh perspective, or returning to basic questions, including "why is this patient failing home therapy?" In this case, undetected cognitive impairment was a significant contributor to her frequent utilization. A hospital/EMS paramedicine partnership facilitated detection and care for this root cause and stopped the frequent ED and 9-1-1 use. This case highlights the impact of superutilizers on EMS, the promising role of intervention teams, and the complexity of cognition/capacity determination in the ED.

Southerland LT, Masters ZA, Brisky T, Stroud J
